Harish: How was the session today?
Jaya: Good, actually. Fourth one. I think I trust her now.
Harish: That's big. Do you want to tell me what you talked about?
Jaya: Not the details. Those stay with her for now. Is that okay?
Harish: Of course. You share what feels right.
Jaya: She said to keep my days steady. So: college, gym at 6, dinner with you guys, lights off by 11.
Jaya: I also changed my route home. The busy road feels safer.
Harish: Smart. Want me to walk with you on Thursdays?
Jaya: Yes please, bhaiya.
Jaya: Weird thing. I thought getting better meant forgetting the accident. It doesn't. I still remember. It just doesn't grab me by the throat every hour anymore.
Harish: That sounds like it's losing its grip.
Jaya: Yeah. Slowly.

qa.q: How many therapy sessions has Jaya had?
qa.a: Four; today was the fourth one.

qa.q: How does Jaya feel about the therapist now?
qa.a: Jaya feels a growing trust and some relief, saying the sessions are going well.

qa.q: What parts of Jaya's approach support her recovery?
qa.a: Putting safety first with a safer route, keeping a steady routine, sharing only what feels right and working with a trained therapist.

qa.q: How might Harish feel when Jaya says the details stay with the therapist?
qa.a: He might feel a flicker of wanting to know, but mostly respect and relief that Jaya is getting proper support.

grounding: Jaya prioritises safety and routine, shares only what feels right and works with a trained therapist, finding that recovery is the past losing its grip, not forgetting.

subtype: Sadness after a loss in children [Actor]
passage:
Saturday
Dadaji died on Tuesday. Today I cried in the morning when I saw his glasses on the shelf. Mummy hugged me for a long time.
Then Joseph from next door came over and we played cricket in the lane. I hit a six over the gate and laughed so much. Then I felt bad for laughing.
At dinner I asked Mummy again, "Is Dadaji really never coming back?" I already asked yesterday. She didn't get cross. She said, "No, beta. His body stopped working. He can't come back. But we can talk about him whenever you want."
She said it's okay to be sad and okay to laugh. Tomorrow is school, like normal. I'm going to keep his glasses in my drawer.
Yogesh

qa.q: What did Yogesh see on the shelf that caused tears?
qa.a: Dadaji's glasses on the shelf.

qa.q: How did Yogesh feel after laughing during cricket?
qa.a: Yogesh felt guilty for laughing, even though the game had been fun, because Dadaji had just died.

qa.q: What did Mummy do that could help any grieving child?
qa.a: She answered the repeated question honestly and simply without getting cross, said both sadness and laughter are okay, and kept the normal routine.

qa.q: What is it like for Mummy when Yogesh asks the same question again?
qa.a: She is likely grieving too and finds it painful, but she stays patient and gentle.

grounding: Yogesh cries, plays happily and asks the same question again after Dadaji's death, and Mummy gives honest, simple words and routine.

passage:
Two months after her brother Manpreet died in the road accident, Gurpreet was back at school. At lunch in the canteen, Wasim did his funny impression of the PT teacher, and Gurpreet laughed out loud. Then she stopped, cheeks burning. How could she laugh?
In the counsellor's room that afternoon, she said it all. "Some days I'm so angry at him for riding in the rain. Then I feel guilty for being angry. And today I laughed."
Mrs D'Souza listened. "Grief comes in waves. Laughing doesn't mean you loved him less. It sounds like the sadness is still about Manpreet, and you still enjoy hockey and your friends."
Gurpreet nodded.
"If the sadness starts spreading to everything, or you feel worthless, come and tell me that same day. We'll keep meeting every Friday."

qa.q: What was Wasim doing when Gurpreet laughed?
qa.a: His funny impression of the PT teacher.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet feel right after laughing?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and guilty, her cheeks burning, as if laughing meant she didn't care about her brother.

qa.q: What did Mrs D'Souza do that supported Gurpreet?
qa.a: She listened, explained that grief comes in waves and laughter is okay, set regular meetings and told her what signs would need extra attention.

qa.q: How might Wasim feel if he knew why Gurpreet stopped laughing?
qa.a: He might feel awkward or worried he'd upset her, though he probably helped her by bringing a moment of lightness.

grounding: Gurpreet feels sadness, anger, guilt and shame at laughing after her brother's death, and a counsellor explains grief's waves and when it needs more attention.

passage:
Five months after his mother's funeral in Osaka, Kaito had stopped going to lectures. His flat smelled of old takeaway. Leila, his classmate, came by with notes and found him still in bed at two in the afternoon.
"I'm useless," he said. "I can't do anything. And honestly, I don't see the point of living without her."
Leila put the notes down and sat on the floor by the bed. Her heart was pounding. "Kaito, thank you for telling me. Are you thinking about ending your life?"
"Sometimes."
"Then I'm staying with you, and we're calling the university counselling line right now. Together."
He didn't argue. She dialled on speaker and stayed while he talked. The counsellor arranged an urgent appointment that afternoon. Leila walked him there. On the way she said, "Missing her this much makes sense. But this heaviness needs more than just time."

qa.q: What time did Leila find Kaito still in bed?
qa.a: At two in the afternoon.

qa.q: How was Kaito feeling five months after the funeral?
qa.a: He felt hopeless and worthless, unable to function, and said he didn't see the point of living without his mother.

qa.q: Why was Leila's response the right one?
qa.a: She took his words seriously, asked directly, stayed with him and got professional help that same afternoon instead of waiting.

qa.q: What was it like for Leila when Kaito said he didn't see the point of living?
qa.a: She was frightened, with her heart pounding, but she stayed calm and present for him.

grounding: Leila notices Kaito months after his loss cannot function and speaks of not wanting to live, and she stays and gets him professional help at once.

passage:
Dear Amma,
I got back from Salma's home in Malappuram last night. I wanted to tell you about it.
When her father died, the whole street came. Neighbours cooked for three days; nobody let the family light their stove. The men and women prayed, and people sat with them for hours, just being there.
But some relatives kept telling Salma, "Be strong. Don't cry in front of your mother." Each time, she went stiff and quiet. I watched her sit alone in the back room.
Then her old aunt came in, sat beside her and said, "Tell me about the time your father fell in the pond." Salma laughed and then cried properly, for the first time. The aunt just held her.
I did what the aunt did. I asked about him. I didn't hurry her. I think it's the most useful thing I've done all year.
Your Lakshmi

qa.q: How many days did neighbours cook for Salma's family?
qa.a: Three days.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi feel watching Salma sit alone in the back room?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt sad and worried for Salma, noticing how the "be strong" comments seemed to isolate her.

qa.q: Which response helped Salma, and why?
qa.a: Her aunt's invitation to talk about her father, without hurrying her, let Salma laugh and cry, unlike the relatives who told her to be strong.

qa.q: How might Salma have felt when relatives told her not to cry?
qa.a: She probably felt lonely and shut in with her grief, going stiff and quiet and withdrawing to the back room.

grounding: Lakshmi observes how shared rites and meals give structure to Salma's loss, how "be strong" isolates her, and how letting her cry and speak of her father helps.

passage:
In the small town of Nanded, Hemant, fifteen, spent his evenings scrolling through photos of gym boys online, every one of them smooth and perfect. He knew some were edited. It didn't help.
He stopped taking his shirt off at the river with friends. He turned the bathroom mirror slightly so he couldn't see himself. When his cousin's wedding came, he told his mother he had a stomach ache and stayed home.
"If I looked different, people would actually like me," he wrote in his notebook.
His sister Parul found him in the dark with his phone, still scrolling at midnight. "You didn't come to the wedding. You don't go to the river. Is this about how you look?"
Hemant said nothing for a long time. Then, "I can't stop thinking about it. All day."
"Then let's tell someone who knows how to help," Parul said. The next morning they went to the school counsellor together.

qa.q: What did Hemant do to the bathroom mirror?
qa.a: He turned it slightly so he couldn't see himself.

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling when he wrote in his notebook?
qa.a: He felt worthless and insecure, believing people would only like him if he looked different.

qa.q: Why was it right for Hemant to seek help?
qa.a: Because the thoughts about his body were taking over his whole day and making him avoid friends and family events, not just ordinary bad feelings.

qa.q: How does Parul see her brother's change?
qa.a: Parul notices his missed wedding and river trips, feels worried, and cares enough to gently ask and go with him for help.

grounding: Hemant compares himself to edited images, avoids mirrors and gatherings and links worth to looks, and seeks help when the thoughts take over his day.

passage:
The school trip bus to Mahabaleshwar left at six, and there was no time for breakfast. Charu noticed that Ankita didn't touch the sandwiches either at the stop or at lunch. "Not hungry," Ankita said, again, and hid her packed lunch in her bag.
It had been like this for weeks. Ankita talked constantly about "fixing" her shape and went quiet if anyone offered food.
Charu wanted to say, "You're fine, just eat." She didn't. At the viewpoint, away from the others, she said, "I've noticed you're skipping meals a lot. I'm not judging you. I just care about you and I'm worried."
Ankita's eyes filled. "Please don't tell anyone."
"I care too much to keep it secret. Let's tell Mrs Pinto together."
That evening on the bus back, Mrs Pinto sat with Ankita and called her mother to plan a doctor's visit.

qa.q: Where did the school trip bus go?
qa.a: To Mahabaleshwar.

qa.q: What was Charu feeling when she chose her words at the viewpoint?
qa.a: She felt worried and caring, and careful not to judge Ankita or comment on her body.

qa.q: What did Charu do well, and why was it wiser than "just eat"?
qa.a: She spoke privately with care and concern, avoided body comments or forcing food, and brought in a trusted teacher the same day so medical support could follow.

qa.q: How might Ankita feel when Charu says she won't keep it secret?
qa.a: She might feel scared and exposed at first, and also a little relieved that someone noticed and cared.

grounding: Charu notices a friend's skipped meals, secrecy and talk about shape, expresses care without body comments, and brings in an adult for medical support.

passage:
In his final year at the college in Sangli, Deepak's father fell ill, the exams moved up, and everything felt out of his hands. Food became the one thing he could control.
He made rules. No eating before evening. Only certain foods. He ate in secret, alone, then felt ashamed. When he followed his rules, he felt a rush of relief, calm, almost proud.
But he was dizzy at cricket practice. He couldn't focus in class. He snapped at his sister Reena when she put a plate in front of him.
One evening Reena found him sitting on the steps, pale. "I'm not going to fight about food," she said quietly. "I'm scared for you. Let's see the doctor at the district hospital tomorrow."
Deepak stared at the ground. "It's the only thing that feels in my control."
"I know. The doctor can help with that too." He nodded.

qa.q: Where did Deepak feel dizzy?
qa.a: At cricket practice.

qa.q: Why did following his food rules feel good to Deepak?
qa.a: He felt a rush of relief and calm, almost proud, because food was the one thing he could control while everything else felt out of his hands.

qa.q: What was Reena's wise choice, and why?
qa.a: She didn't fight about food but shared her worry and suggested the district hospital doctor, the right place to start.

qa.q: How does Reena see Deepak's behaviour?
qa.a: She sees it as something harmful that scares her, not as stubbornness, and she wants him to get proper help.

grounding: Deepak uses rigid food rules and secret eating to cope with stress and a need for control, finding relief but real harm, and his sister steers him to a doctor.

passage:
Dear Payal Didi,
I wanted to say thank you for Sunday.
You know how every family lunch goes. Chachi says I've "grown healthy". Mama's friend praises me when I look thinner. Someone always watches what's on my plate. For years I've felt eyes on me at every meal. I started thinking my looks were the only thing people noticed.
On Sunday, when Chachi started again, you said, "Arohi just topped her engineering exam. Let's talk about that." And later, "We don't comment on anyone's body at this table. Only on how the food tastes."
Everyone laughed a bit awkwardly. But nobody watched my plate for the rest of the lunch. I ate without thinking about it for the first time in ages.
You made the whole table kinder. I won't forget it.
Love,
Arohi

qa.q: What did Payal Didi say Arohi had just done?
qa.a: Topped the engineering exam.

qa.q: How has Arohi felt at family meals for years?
qa.a: Arohi has felt watched and self-conscious, believing appearance was the only thing people valued.

qa.q: What changed the climate at the table?
qa.a: Payal Didi's kindness in shifting the talk to Arohi's achievement and setting a rule against body comments.

qa.q: How might Chachi have felt when Payal Didi spoke up?
qa.a: Chachi may have felt a little embarrassed or caught out, even if the comments were meant kindly.

grounding: Arohi, used to teasing and praise about appearance and feeling watched at meals, finds that a cousin's kindness and talk away from looks change the climate.

subtype: Building a kinder relationship with the body [Response]
passage:
Thanks for having me, Hafsa. So I'm Jomon, and for most of college I hated my body. I stood in front of the mirror listing everything wrong.
The change started on a trek in Munnar. At the top, legs shaking, I thought: this body just carried me up a mountain. It didn't care what I looked like.
After that I unfollowed every account that made me feel bad. I started eating regular meals instead of skipping and then bingeing. And I tried talking to myself like I'd talk to a friend. "You're tired, you did well today," instead of "You're disgusting."
But honestly, the biggest step was when I told my doctor how bad it had got. She referred me to a counsellor who specialises in this. The trek helped. The professional help is what really changed things.

qa.q: Where did Jomon's change start?
qa.a: On a trek in Munnar.

qa.q: How did Jomon feel at the top of the trek?
qa.a: Jomon felt amazed and grateful, realising the body had just carried them up a mountain.

qa.q: What steps from Jomon's story build a kinder relationship with the body?
qa.a: Valuing what the body can do, unfollowing harsh accounts, eating regular meals, speaking kindly to oneself, and getting a qualified professional when the struggle is serious.

qa.q: How might the doctor have seen Jomon's honesty?
qa.a: The doctor likely saw it as a brave and important step and responded by referring Jomon to a specialist counsellor.

grounding: Jomon values what the body can do, limits harsh social media, eats regular meals and speaks kindly to self, and gets professional help for a serious struggle.
